title: Gold Just Had Its Worst Week Since March. The Safe-Haven Trade Is Breaking in Real Time.
excerpt: Gold fell 4.9 per cent in a single week and is down 18.5 per cent from its January record high — during the biggest geopolitical crisis in decades. The metal that NRIs have treated as an insurance policy is behaving like a liability. Here is why, and what to do about it.
body:
Gold hit $5,318.40 an ounce in January 2026, its highest price in history. Since then it has done something that has confounded millions of investors worldwide: it has fallen during a war.

On Friday, Comex gold settled at $4,337.10, down 3.1 per cent on the day and 4.9 per cent for the week — its sharpest weekly decline since March. It is now 18.5 per cent below its record high. Silver has been even more brutal, crashing 8.8 per cent in a week and nearly 40 per cent from its January peak.

For a metal whose entire reputation rests on being the ultimate safe haven during geopolitical crises, this is the wrong way around. And for NRI families who hold significant gold — culturally, emotionally, financially — the implications demand serious attention.

Why Gold Is Falling During a War

The answer is oil. The US-Iran conflict has kept the Strait of Hormuz effectively closed since late February, disrupting a fifth of the world's crude supply. Brent crude traded near $95 a barrel last week, with Exxon's senior vice president warning it could spike to $150 or $160 if inventories keep draining.

High oil prices feed directly into inflation expectations. And inflation expectations drive interest rate expectations. On Friday, a blockbuster US jobs report — 172,000 new jobs versus the 80,000 forecast — pushed the probability of a Federal Reserve rate hike to 70 per cent by year-end. The 10-year Treasury yield surged past 4.5 per cent.

Gold does not pay interest. When Treasury bonds yield 4.5 per cent, the opportunity cost of holding gold rises sharply. The stronger dollar that accompanies rate-hike expectations compounds the damage. This is the chain that Commerzbank analyst Carsten Fritsch described when he cut his end-2026 gold forecast from $5,000 to $4,800 this week:

War → oil shock → inflation → rate hike expectations → stronger dollar → weaker gold.

It is counterintuitive but mechanically straightforward. Gold rises when real rates fall and the dollar weakens. The oil shock has reversed both simultaneously.

The Turkey Signal

The first cracks appeared in March, when Turkey's central bank sold and swapped $3 billion worth of gold reserves in a single week to stabilise the lira. That was not the behaviour of an institution adding protection. It was the behaviour of an institution raising dollars in a liquidity crunch.

When major regional players start treating gold as collateral rather than a trophy, supply floods the market at precisely the moment when headlines would normally support the price.

What India's Government Has Done

India — the world's second-largest gold consumer — has moved aggressively. Last month, the government raised import duties on gold and silver to 15 per cent from 6 per cent, aiming to reduce overseas purchases and ease pressure on foreign exchange reserves strained by oil imports.

The result: Indian gold demand has collapsed. Dealers are quoting discounts of up to $87 an ounce over official domestic prices. India's physically backed gold ETFs recorded their first net monthly outflow in a year in May. The wedding season, traditionally a peak period for gold buying, is ending with subdued demand across the country.

For NRIs who send money home or plan gold purchases around Indian weddings, the landscape has shifted materially. The 15 per cent import duty means that Indian gold prices already carry a massive premium over international spot. If spot prices fall further — as rate-hike expectations suggest — the value of gold held in India could face pressure from both directions.

What NRI Investors Should Do

The consensus among analysts is not that gold is dead. JPMorgan still forecasts prices approaching $5,000 by end-2026, driven by long-term central bank demand. Commerzbank sees $4,800. The metal absorbed a sharp move to $5,400 earlier this year despite every headwind.

But the short-term picture is hostile. The test, as one analyst framed it, is straightforward: if regional dollar funding stabilises and demand stops unwinding, the selloff can compress quickly. If real-rate pressure remains firm, bounces stay vulnerable.

For NRI portfolios, the practical implications are:

Do not panic-sell physical gold. The cultural and long-term store-of-value case for gold has not changed. But recognise that gold is no longer acting as a hedge against geopolitical risk. It is acting as a rate-sensitive asset.

Avoid adding to gold positions at current prices unless you are a very long-term holder. The rate environment is working against you, and the India duty structure means your rupee-denominated gold is doubly penalised.

Consider the opportunity cost. With US Treasuries yielding 4.5 per cent and Indian government bonds offering similar returns, the case for parking capital in a non-yielding asset has weakened considerably.

Watch the Hormuz negotiations. If a deal reopens the strait, oil falls, rate-hike probabilities ease, and gold likely rebounds sharply. If talks collapse, oil spikes higher, rates rise further, and gold faces more downside. The binary outcome makes timing treacherous.

Gold remains a permanent fixture of Indian financial culture. But culture and markets operate on different timescales. Right now, the market is repricing gold in real time, and the safe-haven narrative is not holding.
